rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing late peaks. The retention window will guide narrower, faster gradients in subsequent injections.
Keep the gradient unchanged and raise temperature to test selectivity of the sole critical pair. Higher temperature should also shorten retention, leaving room for a shallower gradient if needed.
Injection 2 reached the maximum CRF, so test a shorter gradient to reduce analysis time while retaining full resolution. The first pair, currently at R = 1.67, is the limiting check.

Narrow the gradient window to recover resolution of the first pair while keeping the 10-minute gradient. This slope lies between injections 2 and 3 and should preserve full elution with a shorter last-peak time than injection 2.

Shift the window upward while preserving injection 4's gradient slope to test whether initial retention can be trimmed without losing first-pair resolution. Injection 4 remains the fully resolved fallback.

Restore the low starting organic fraction and use a slope only slightly steeper than injection 4 to target full resolution with earlier elution. The final organic fraction remains above the last peak's estimated elution fraction of 0.57.

Test a slightly steeper slope to approach the first pair's resolution limit while shortening the programmed gradient. The last peak may enter the final hold, so this run will establish whether the lower endpoint offsets the time savings.

The 60 C methods are near the first pair's resolution limit, with injection 7 retaining maximum CRF. Test the opposite temperature extreme for a possible selectivity reversal that could support a faster gradient; the broad endpoint helps ensure complete elution.

Test whether a modest temperature increase separates the late cluster seen at 25 C while preserving the improved early-pair selectivity. The shorter gradient explores a faster alternative to the fully resolved 60 C methods.

Raise temperature modestly to spread the late cluster and shift the starting organic fraction upward to shorten retention. This tests whether the lower-temperature selectivity branch can yield a faster fully resolved method than injection 7.

Increase the starting organic fraction by one step to probe early-pair selectivity at 35 C while slightly reducing gradient steepness. The late pairs were resolved in injection 10, so the main test is whether the first pair improves without becoming effectively unretained.

Return to the successful high-temperature branch and make the gradient shallower than injection 5 to recover first-pair resolution. The higher starting fraction may offset the slower slope, potentially matching full resolution with a shorter last-peak time.

Reduce the slope from 0.075 to 0.070 organic fraction per minute to bring the first pair above R = 1.5. This tests a fully resolved alternative starting at higher organic fraction, with all peaks expected comfortably before 10 minutes.

Test a slope of 0.085 per minute, just steeper than injection 7, to locate the fastest fully resolved boundary. The higher endpoint also keeps the last peak inside the gradient rather than in the final hold.

Test a shallower gradient at 30 C to separate the late cluster while retaining the stronger early-pair selectivity seen at lower temperature. The elevated starting fraction offsets some added retention; injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Reduce the slope relative to injection 10 to improve its limiting early pair, while retaining 35 C to separate the late cluster. This tests a lower-temperature route to maximum CRF, with the last peak expected before 10 minutes.

Use a shallower slope than injection 16 to bring its first pair above R = 1.5 while preserving late-pair separation. Comparison with injection 15 also isolates the temperature effect and tests a lower-temperature maximum-CRF alternative.

Test a trimmed endpoint with the same slope as injection 2, targeting its stronger first-pair resolution while keeping all peaks within the gradient. This offers a larger resolution margin than injection 7 while retaining maximum CRF if the last peak remains before 10 minutes.

Test a shallower gradient to increase the first pair's resolution margin while targeting a last peak before 10 minutes. Monitor the third–fourth pair, whose resolution has decreased as the gradient becomes shallower; injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Shift injection 19's window upward while preserving its slope to shorten retention and improve the third–fourth pair's separation. The first pair should retain more resolution margin than in injection 13, targeting a robust maximum-CRF alternative.

Shorten injection 20's gradient while keeping the slope slightly shallower than injection 13, which achieved full resolution. This should preserve maximum CRF with the last peak around 7.3 minutes and inside the gradient.

Test a slope of 0.0625 per minute, near the balance between the two limiting early pairs in injection 19. With maximum CRF already achieved, this targets greater resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes; injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Use an intermediate slope between injections 18 and 22 to target a larger resolution margin than the fastest method while shortening retention relative to injection 22. All peaks should remain inside the gradient and elute before 10 minutes, preserving maximum CRF.

Test a slope of 0.0708 per minute, slightly steeper than injection 13, to shorten its last-peak time while targeting first-pair resolution just above 1.5. Injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Finish with a slope between injections 18 and 23, targeting maximum CRF with a useful first-pair resolution margin and all peaks before 10 minutes. Injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
